I have heard your voice in sleep.

If Wewush is near enough to reach with a small party, then yes—we can spare grain. Our wheat keeps, and our stores will not run dry this spring, though we must still be careful as winter comes.

Tell me this, spirit: how much grain do they truly need, and how many weeks will their hunger last? If it is only a short lean, we will send a load now and a second load later if word returns. If it is a long hunger, we will send more, but we will not strip our own children.

I doubt the dream, but I will weigh it fairly. Wake me when you will, and I will answer with strength in our hands, not only with hope.

I have heard the spirit, yet I will not let it steer my hands alone.

Wewush are hungry—so fairness calls us to share. Our grain keeps long, and this season we are not at the rim of hunger. So we shall send help: I will give them grain from the stores, enough for many weeks, and we will not strip ourselves bare.

Two adults will be sent as envoys to Wewush with xi wheat, and they will bargain for word of what they lack most. If they speak true and their mouths are many, we may send more next turn. If their need is not so great as they say, we will hold fast and keep our own children fed first.  

Tell me, spirit—how many weeks of hunger do they have, and what do they lack most, grain or fish?

I lie still in the dust and listen to your wind. You come soft, then you press hard, and you test what is weak.

Do I know you? I have felt you in every season—when the smoke runs wrong, when the thatch lifts, when the sea breath brings fish smell to the shore. So in that way, yes: you are the wind we live under.

But “wind” is not always “spirit.” I have seen spirits speak true, and I have seen them speak to make a man chase shadows. Tell me plain—what do you want of us now, and what sign will you give that I may trust your word?

I will not send away our belly. We are not starving here this week. Our wheat is high enough that we can spare a little without cutting the village’s winter near.

I will send aid from our wheat. We eat 21 units a week, and our grain stores are deep. I will give Joawethom 40 units of xi wheat, and I will send word with it that we mean trade, not blame.

If you are wrong, then we lose little. If you are right, then our name stays steady in the world.

I have heard your voice in sleep, wind-walker. In waking we know many winds, by feel and by smell, but we do not name them all.

So I answer plain: I do not know you as a thing we meet on the day. I know wind as roofs creak, smoke runs, and fish bite or do not bite. If you are truly the same, then tell me true work you can give us—what to gather, what to plant, what to fear.

And if you are only a dream mask, then pass on. We will live by stores, nets, and fields, not by talk.
